performers: Lukas Foss, piano; Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York; Leonard Bernstein
recorded: 27 February 1950, New York; issued as Columbia ML 4325
intro: Bernstein conducts the Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York, with Lukas Foss as soloist, in a recording made in February 1950, within a year of the first performance of his Second Symphony, The Age of Anxiety. Part I contains the Prologue and the two sets of seven variations.

cues.title: Prologue, two clarinets
cues.text: The Prologue opens with a pianissimo duet for two clarinets, one overlapping and echoing the other. A long descending scale for flute follows. Bernstein said this scale is the bridge to the unconscious, where most of the poem takes place.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note for the first performance, as quoted on the Leonard Bernstein Office’s page for the symphony. The Prologue is the first section in the section list of the Internet Archive transfer note. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Seven Ages, opening
cues.text: The Seven Ages opens with a piano solo, followed by a series of variations. Bernstein wrote that “each variation seizes upon some feature of the preceding one and develops it.”
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note, quoted on the Bernstein Office page. The start of The Seven Ages at about 2:21 is given in the transfer note’s section list, and the first piano entries appear in the audio at that point. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation 3 and the tempo marks
cues.text: Variation 3, marked Largamente, ma mosso, begins at about 4:38. The seven variations are marked L’istesso tempo, Poco più mosso, Largamente ma mosso, Più mosso, Agitato, Poco meno mosso and L’istesso tempo.
cues.evidence: The tempo marks are those printed in the track list of the Hyperion booklet for CDA67170 (Hamelin, Ulster Orchestra, Sitkovetsky), https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/67170-B.pdf . The transfer note gives the approximate start time. https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Auden’s poem, 1947
cues.text: W. H. Auden’s poem The Age of Anxiety appeared in July 1947 and won the Pulitzer Prize in 1948. Its four characters, Malin, Quant, Emble and Rosetta, meet in a New York bar in wartime. Bernstein took Auden’s six section titles for his movements.
cues.evidence: Leonard Bernstein Office, page for Symphony No. 2: the poem’s publication, prize, characters and the six titles. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety

cues.title: The Seven Stages, Variations 8 to 14
cues.text: The Seven Stages, Variations 8 to 14, follows the characters of Auden’s poem on a symbolic dream-quest in search of “that state of prehistoric happiness”.
cues.evidence: The start at about 10:41 comes from the transfer note’s section list and agrees with a break in the audio at that point. The description of the section is the Bernstein Office’s summary of the poem. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation 9, Tempo di Valse
cues.text: Variation 9 begins at about 12:29. It is marked Più mosso (Tempo di Valse). The Hyperion booklet describes it as a waltz related to the passacaglia theme of Variation 8.
cues.evidence: The marking and the description are from the track list and note of the Hyperion booklet for CDA67170, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/67170-B.pdf . The approximate start time is from the section list in the Internet Archive transfer note. https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Variation 14, end of Part I
cues.text: Variation 14, the last of Part I, begins at about 16:04. Bernstein described the end of The Seven Stages as “a hectic, though indecisive, close”. Part II follows with the Dirge.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note, quoted on the Bernstein Office page and printed on the back of the Columbia LP sleeve; the start of Variation 14 from the transfer note, which agrees with a change in the audio at that point. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Lukas Foss (piano), Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York (orchestra), Leonard Bernstein (conductor)
fields.note: The Internet Archive note, the Shellackophile post and the Discogs credits agree. Individual players are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original 1949 version; Bernstein revised the finale in 1965
fields.note: The Internet Archive note and the Shellackophile post identify this recording as the original version, made before the 1965 revision of the Epilogue.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Recording date given in the Internet Archive note and in the Shellackophile post, which are by the same transferor. The Leonard Bernstein Office confirms the month (February 1950) but not the day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Columbia’s 30th Street Studio, New York City
fields.note: Named in the Internet Archive note.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Mono vinyl LP; the Discogs entry for the US mono LP is a blue-label early pressing.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: ML 4325 (LP); the 78-rpm set MM-946, records 13121-D to 13124-D, was issued at the same time
fields.note: The transferred copy is described as a c. 1960 pressing of the LP, not the 78-rpm set.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: LP side A (Part I). The 78-rpm issue carried this music on sides 1 to 4, matrices XCO 42387 to 42390
fields.note: The 78-rpm matrices are those listed in the Internet Archive note. LP matrix, take and stamper numbers are not given.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Transfer by Bryan of The Shellackophile, from a mono LP
fields.note: The Internet Archive note refers to ‘my copy’ of the LP; the blog post is signed Bryan. Individual mastering credits are not stated.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Shellackophile blog post offering this transfer is dated 8 October 2012 and the Internet Archive item was added on 11 April 2022. Neither date is established as the date of transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: FLAC and VBR MP3 derivatives of a mono LP transfer
fields.note: Equalisation, noise reduction and speed correction are not documented. The research desk measured the pitch of the file at about A = 441 Hz, which is consistent with normal LP speed (inference from the audio).

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Copyrighted Bernstein composition; performance licences through Boosey & Hawkes, according to the Leonard Bernstein Office
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial publication before 1963; the LP ML 4325 was reviewed in The American Record Guide of January 1951
fields.note: The American Record Guide, January 1951, reviews Columbia ML 4325 at $4.85, and The New Records, March 1951, reviews both the LP and the 78-rpm album MM-946. The Internet Archive note gives first issue in March 1951, which the January 1951 review shows to be too late for the LP; Discogs dates the US LP to 1950. Any of these years is before 1963. The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not US or worldwide clearance, not a Creative Commons licence and not a US-government recording. Rights in the composition are separate.

quote.text: This will be our reply to violence: to make music more intensely, more beautifully, more devotedly than ever before.
quote.source: Bernstein, remarks at Madison Square Garden, 25 November 1963; printed in Findings (1982)

composer.background:
Leonard Bernstein was born on 25 August 1918 in Lawrence, Massachusetts, the eldest of three children of Samuel and Jennie Bernstein, Jewish immigrants from Ukraine. The family moved to Boston when he was a few months old, and his father sold hairdressing and beauty supplies. In the autumn of 1928 an aunt gave the family an upright piano, and the ten-year-old Leonard began to pick out songs on it. Samuel Bernstein, who wanted his son to join the business, agreed to lessons. The New Yorker reported in 1958 that he had said backstage at Tanglewood: “someday I suppose the books will say, ‘Lenny Bernstein had a father.’” In October 1932 Bernstein began lessons with Helen Coates, an assistant to the Boston pianist Heinrich Gebhard.

He attended Boston Latin School and entered Harvard in 1935, where his teachers included Walter Piston and Edward Burlingame Hill. In January 1937 he met the conductor Dimitri Mitropoulos at a reception and spent the following week at Mitropoulos’s Boston Symphony rehearsals. On 14 November of that year he met Aaron Copland at a dance recital in New York. He graduated in June 1939.
